chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
title: The difference between Milwaukee and New York, and the myth of regional styles
summary: Playing with the New York pros was easier; he says Chicago style does not exist and he played his way back in Ohio.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

How did you feel about it?

It's like Condon said -- there's a great difference between class and ass - you know - that's one of his remarks, but - you know - the difference between playing in Milwaukee and then going to New York and playing with all the pros--- what a difference - it was just--- it was so easy to work with the pros---
Did you find that you fitted right in - you had no problems right?
Well, I did in the beginning as I told you ---
Yeah but aside from just not knowing the tunes---

Yeah but the difference between Chicago style, which there is no such thing -- and New York style and New Orleans style -- look, I come from Ohio and I played that way long before I went to Chicago or New York or anything -- but, apparently, I was playing the right way - the right kind of jazz and, I mean, you know, this is a thing that the critics put on you. I'm in Chicago so I play Chicago style, but I told you the difference in the two -- Dixie Land - things -- and Chicago played off-the-cuff music from the pop songs and the New Orleans jazz kind of New York jazz were playing Dixie Land songs---
